title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page, §38 of E449, proves Theorem 38: for every prime P there is an integer a such that the powers 1, a, a^2, ... mod P run through all P−1 nonzero residues before 1 recurs. In modern terms, the multiplicative group (Z/PZ)^* is cyclic and a primitive root exists.

The argument runs as follows.
(i) For any x < P, Fermat gives x^{P−1} ≡ 1 (mod P), so the residues of powers of x are periodic with period dividing P−1.
(ii) It therefore suffices to find a with ord_P(a) = P−1, i.e. a^{P−1} is the lowest power of a congruent to 1. In that case the residues a^0, ..., a^{P−2} are pairwise distinct; otherwise a^i ≡ a^j would give a^{j−i} ≡ 1 at a lower exponent. Being P−1 distinct nonzero residues, they exhaust 1, ..., P−1, so the residue series is 'complete'.
(iii) If some x has x^n ≡ 1 with n < P−1, then n divides P−1. This is §21: the order divides P−1.
(iv) §34–35 showed that the 'form' x^{P−1} − 1 has 'cases proper to it'. These are values x = a for which P divides a^{P−1} − 1 but divides no lower a^d − 1 with d a proper divisor of P−1. Euler obtained this by counting solutions of x^d ≡ 1 for the divisors d.
(v) Hence such an a has order P−1 and generates a complete residue series.

The next page names these a 'radices primitivae', tabulates them for P ≤ 23, and remarks that the existence proof gives no method for finding them. The page itself only assembles earlier lemmas; the real content lies in §§21 and 28–35.
errors: The deduction on this page is logically sound given §21 and §34.

Its validity rests on §§33–35. Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, art. 56) judged Euler's existence proof deficient: the count of 'proper cases' presupposes that x^d ≡ 1 (mod P) has exactly d solutions for each d dividing P−1, and Euler's earlier sections do not adequately establish this. The gap is inherited, not created, here.
The proof is non-constructive, as Euler himself admits on the next page (§39).

ideas.what: Existence of an element of order P−1 modulo a prime P (complete residue series of a geometric progression)
ideas.modern_name: Existence of primitive roots / cyclicity of (Z/pZ)^*
ideas.usually_credited_to: Stated by Lambert (1769); Euler E449 (1774) gave the first attempted proof; Gauss (DA 1801, arts. 52–56) gave the first proof generally considered complete
ideas.where_published: E449, Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 18 (1774); Opera Omnia I.3

ideas.what: Distinctness of a^0, ..., a^{P−2} when the order of a is P−1, so that the powers exhaust all nonzero residues
ideas.modern_name: An element of order |G| generates G

ideas.what: Order of any residue divides P−1 (cited as §21)
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange's theorem for (Z/pZ)^* / order divides p−1

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known primitive-root existence proof. It is extensively discussed by Gauss (DA art. 56), Weil, Sandifer and others, and the origin of the term 'primitive root' is documented. The page only assembles earlier lemmas, so nothing here is new to specialists.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially faithful to the image.
The inequality printed after 'existente n' is an unusual less-than-type glyph; the meaning is n < P−1 (strictly lower power).
